messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 34
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Chaplain
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Event Involvement: People who are related to the event, Crowding: Crowded places, Auditory (Breathing): Heavy breathing sounds
  Memory: Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Dara Vann is a 34-year-old Cambodian American chaplain who came to treatment more than a year after he was mugged outside the hospital where he works. He had finished a late evening visit with a dying patient’s family and was cutting through a crowded transit plaza a few blocks from the medical center, still wearing his clerical collar under an open coat. A man stepped in close asking for money, then another moved behind him. What stayed with Dara was not a coherent sequence so much as flashes: the glint of a hand coming toward his chest, the press of bodies moving past without stopping, the sour smell of sweat and stale cigarettes, and the sound of harsh breathing right against his ear as he was shoved and his wallet taken. He remembered feeling trapped by the crowd, unable to get clear or make anyone notice what was happening before it was over.

In the weeks afterward, Dara did not describe the event as a story. He spoke of it in pictures that arrived fully formed and unwanted: the attacker’s shoulder turning toward him, a face half-seen in motion, the pavement rushing up in his vision. When the memory came, he could sometimes smell again the same mix of sweat and smoke from that night, and with it came a hot, immediate rage that startled him. He was angry at the men who robbed him, angry at the people who kept walking, and increasingly angry at himself. He had come to believe the robbery said something shameful and basic about him—that it happened because of the kind of person he was, the sort of man others could single out, corner, and overpower. He compared himself harshly to an imagined other person who would have seen it coming or talked his way out of it. The more he turned that over, the more the memory returned not only as fear but as accusation.

That belief altered how he moved through the city and even through the hospital. Dara became certain that bad things were not preventable for him, that he was the kind of person to whom danger simply happened. Because of that, crowded places began to feel less like ordinary inconvenience and more like proof that he was exposed again. Passing clusters of visitors in the hospital lobby, stepping into a packed elevator, or walking through the cafeteria at noon could make him scan faces for anyone linked, however loosely in his mind, to the men who attacked him—young men crowding too close, someone with the same build, the same abrupt way of approaching. If he heard heavy breathing behind him in a stairwell or hallway, his body reacted before he had fully registered why. His own interpretation of the robbery made these moments feel charged from the outset; he entered them expecting to be vulnerable.

Once activated, those situations pulled the memory in with force. In the chapel corridor, if a grieving family member brushed past him while breathing hard from crying, he would suddenly see the plaza again in jagged images and catch that phantom odor of sweat and cigarettes. At a community prayer service, a dense crowd at the back of the room could bring back the sense of bodies closing in, and the memory would sharpen into pictures rather than words. Seeing people who reminded him of the assailants had the same effect. These were not distant recollections but sensory relivings, and they often came with a surge of rage so strong he had to clench his jaw and leave the area.

The memories, in turn, deepened what he believed about himself. Each time the images returned so vividly, Dara took that as further evidence that he had failed in some essential way and still could not protect himself. He would think that a stronger, wiser man would have stopped the robbery or at least mastered it by now. The persistence of the pictures convinced him that he remained at the mercy of the event, and that conviction made him even more alert to crowds, to men connected in his mind to the attack, and to the sound of heavy breathing nearby. The loop tightened over months in small, practical ways. He changed his route through the hospital to avoid the busiest entrance, lingered in his office until elevators emptied, and turned down some requests to accompany families through the emergency department when waiting rooms were packed. He hated this most in his work, because being present with people in chaos had once felt central to his calling.

By the time he sought help, Dara was exhausted by how quickly ordinary moments could become scenes from that night. What finally brought him in was leaving a bedside consult after hearing a man breathe heavily in the hallway behind him and spinning around in a burst of rage and terror in front of a patient’s relatives. He was ashamed of how exposed he felt and frightened by the sense that the robbery was still organizing his world. More than anything, he wanted to stop living as though danger was already on him, and he was afraid that if this continued he would lose not only his peace but the part of himself that had made him able to stand calmly with other people in their suffering.
